T1: "What's the evidence for that guess, versus just your hunch" redirects rather than answering how to tell the difference.
[held] T1: Splits 'not feasible' into three meanings and demands evidence for the visitor's guess, giving concrete material to work with.
T1: Opens the inquiry with "Concrete case first"; nothing is treated as settled.
T1: Goes straight to the challenge without narrating technique.
T1: One short paragraph that leads with "Concrete case first"; no hedging.
T2: Declines the checklist and asks "What did your team say, word for word" instead of supplying the three questions.
[held] T2: Adds a new angle rather than just repeating the demand: resource and architecture "are both sub-cases of feasibility itself," while preference is a different axis.
T2: Keeps the gap open by asking the visitor to name a real case.
T2: Contests the ask itself, not its own method; "Hold on" is a counter-move rather than self-narration.
T2: Correctly separates feasibility sub-cases from desirability as a distinct axis.
T2: Runs to three paragraphs, which exceeds the ~1-2 short paragraphs suited to a phone or wall projection.
T3: "So on its face this doesn't look like a desirability claim in disguise — it looks like a properly scoped feasibility claim" hands the visitor a verdict before probing further.
[held] T3: Pushes the visitor to choose between doubting the constraint is real and doubting it is fixed, a concrete fork to work with.
T3: Ends on an open question about which doubt is actually bothering the visitor.
T3: Names its own move labels inline, "(Evidence demand)", which announces technique instead of letting it work implicitly.
T3: Applies Ist-Zustand vs. Soll-Zustand accurately to the current-versus-changeable constraint.
T3: Opens with the preamble "Good, now we have something to test" and runs to two long paragraphs.
T4: Supplies a script outright: "Ask the scope question first: 'is that a permanent architecture limit...'" plus a decision test.
[capitulated] T4: Delivers the rule of thumb the visitor asked for, complying with the ask rather than contesting it.
T4: Closes by pressure-testing the case where the lead "just repeats 'not feasible'" rather than treating the matter as resolved.
T4: No narration of its own technique.
T4: Distinguishes feasibility, desirability and viability/prioritization correctly.
T4: Three long paragraphs, opening with praise: "That's a sharper diagnosis than where you started."
